meta.title: US cancer screening recommendations for average-risk adults
meta.checked_against: The USPSTF recommendation pages on uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org, read on 2026-10-05
meta.scope: Adults at average risk. People with a family history, a known gene change (such as BRCA1/2), earlier cancer, past chest radiation, or other risk factors may be advised differently by their own doctor.
meta.review_status: NOT YET REVIEWED BY A CLINICIAN
meta.not_covered: Only breast, cervical, colorectal, lung and prostate cancer are covered, because they have a general-population screening recommendation from the Task Force that was checked. Nothing here says other cancers cannot be screened for.
known_limitations: Recommendations are revised over time. Each item carries its publication date; a newer version may exist.
Cervical screening depends on whether the cervix is still present. The tool asks.
Lung screening needs pack-years (packs per day times years smoked), which people often estimate poorly.
The Task Force's grade describes the strength of evidence for average-risk people. It is not a personal prediction.

items.source: USPSTF, Breast Cancer: Screening, April 30 2024 (Grade B)
USPSTF, Cervical Cancer: Screening, August 21 2018 (Grade A)

items.test: stool test or a look inside the bowel
items.source: USPSTF, Colorectal Cancer: Screening, May 18 2021 (Grade A for 50 to 75, Grade B for 45 to 49, Grade C for 76 to 85)

items.test: low-dose CT scan of the chest
items.source: USPSTF, Lung Cancer: Screening, March 9 2021 (Grade B)
USPSTF, Prostate Cancer: Screening, May 8 2018 (Grade C for 55 to 69, Grade D for 70 and older)

colorectal_tests: a stool test (FIT or a sensitive guaiac test) every year
a stool DNA test with FIT every 1 to 3 years
a flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years plus a yearly FIT
